Alexei Petrov

life-034 · development · fictional age 16

Written life first, then interpreted by a separate response author without the engine or results. These are synthetic checks. There is no correct career answer key.

Life from age 4 to 16

I like finding something in the numbers that changes what a group decides, especially if we can go outside and see whether it worked. I also need movement in my day; understanding something does not always mean I want to sit still with it.

  • family: Lives with parents and a younger sister; grandparents join video calls regularly.
  • finances: Moderate income with steady employment and a limited travel budget.
  • geography: San Antonio, Texas; moved from Bulgaria with family at five.
  • cultureLanguages: Bulgarian and English; family maintains food and holiday traditions.
  • school: Public high school with broad electives and an active student recreation program.
  • accessOpportunities: City facilities, school advising, and local college outreach.
  • Age 4–5

    In 2014, Alexei liked making miniature obstacle courses for toy cars and listening to grandparents tell familiar stories. He remembered the funny details more than the order of events, often insisting on retelling the stories his own way.

  • Age 6–7

    At five in 2015, his family moved to Texas for a parent’s work. By 2017, he was comfortable speaking English at school and Bulgarian at home, while discovering that the same joke did not always travel well between them.

  • Age 8–9

    In 2018, adults encouraged chess because he liked puzzles, but Alexei found long matches tedious. He preferred a beginner dance class and neighborhood basketball, where he could make a quick decision and immediately try something different.

  • Age 10–11

    During 2020, he helped cook family meals and filmed short dance sequences with his sister. Repeating a section for the camera taught him to notice small timing errors, though he still disliked replaying ordinary family videos.

  • Age 12–13

    At twelve, Alexei joined a school recreation committee and helped compare options for unused outdoor space. In 2023, he discovered an interest in maps and data when a simple attendance chart challenged the committee’s confident assumptions about popular activities.

  • Age 14–15

    Across 2024 and 2025, he worked occasional shifts at a recreation-center snack counter and took a statistics elective. He liked finding patterns but sometimes jumped to an explanation before checking whether the data collection itself had changed.

  • Age 16

    At sixteen in 2026, Alexei is exploring Texas summer programs in movement, data, and urban spaces. He wants to meet a wider range of people, while remaining unsure whether formal analytical coursework would suit him as well as the practical questions that sparked his curiosity.

Life now

  • enjoys: Dance timing · Basketball · Maps of shared spaces
  • avoids: Long chess matches · Being introduced through a cultural stereotype
  • activities: Recreation committee · Snack-counter shifts · Statistics elective
  • demonstratedSkills: Coordinates movement · Reads simple data displays · Welcomes new participants
  • unfamiliarActivities: Advanced programming · Long residential programs
  • motivations: Active collaboration · Evidence that changes a decision
  • ambitions: Sample unfamiliar analytical work · He imagines adulthood in a lively neighborhood with friends nearby, regular movement, and occasional travel to family.
  • struggles: Premature explanations · Loses patience with slow meetings
  • supports: Parents · Sister · Statistics teacher · Recreation supervisor
  • practicalConstraints: Work shifts · Travel budget · Competing program dates

Still uncertain: Will analytical interest survive less immediately practical material? · How much structure helps him stay engaged without feeling confined?
